old: It once simply named the loose, gritty ground people stood on, before it named the ground beneath a spectacle.
Its Latin ancestor meant "sand" — the very stuff scattered across the floor of ancient contests.
Compare Sabine fasēna, a cousin word for the same sandy ground that gave us this term.
clues: This kind of venue for crowds takes its name from a Latin word that simply meant sand, the gritty ground underfoot.
An enclosed space with tiered seats around a central floor for sports, concerts or shows, usually roofed and smaller than a stadium. In Latin it named an amphitheater's sand-covered floor.
It also means any field of fierce competition, as when a newcomer steps into the political one. Hockey and basketball teams often play their home games in one downtown.
